summary: This informational memo records a joint IAB and IESG recommendation for restructuring IETF administration. The IETF Chair declared consensus to follow it in November 2004. It led to the IASA described in RFC 4071.

plainLanguage.summary: The IETF decided to reorganise how it handles its business tasks. This document records the plan that the leaders suggested and the community agreed to.

subtitle: How the IETF chose to reorganize its business operations.

tldr.problem: By 2004, the IETF needed to change how its administrative support functions (meetings, contracts, finances) were handled. The existing arrangement with the Internet Society was not meeting needs effectively.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB and IESG studied several proposals and recommended Scenario O: keeping administrative functions within the Internet Society's legal structure but giving the IETF direct control through a new oversight committee (the IAOC) and a dedicated IETF Administrative Director.
tldr.outcome: The IETF community accepted this recommendation in November 2004. RFC 4071 later formalized the resulting structure, creating the IETF Administrative Support Activity (IASA), which has since managed all IETF operations.

today: RFC 4089 is informational and has not been obsoleted. It records a pivotal decision that led to RFC 4071, which formalized the IASA structure. The IASA, built on the foundation of Scenario O, has successfully managed IETF operations for nearly two decades and continues to do so.

sections.title: The Problem: Why Reorganize?
sections.content:
RFC 4089 records a joint recommendation from the IAB (Internet Architecture Board) and the IESG (Internet Engineering Steering Group) for restructuring the IETF's administrative functions. The root issue was simple: the IETF needed support functions—arranging meetings, managing contracts with vendors, handling finances, overseeing the RFC Editor and IANA relationships—but the way these functions were being provided in 2004 was not working well.

The IETF had been an activity of the Internet Society (ISOC), and ISOC provided these administrative services. However, questions arose about whether the arrangement served the IETF's needs. The dialogue and debate in 2003 and 2004 led the IAB and IESG to conclude that the approach needed to change. RFC 3716, titled "The IETF in the Large: Administration and Execution," had outlined the problem and called for action.
sections.plainLanguage: The group that runs the IETF realized its office work was not being handled well. They needed to fix how business tasks were done.

sections.title: The Evaluation Process and Scenarios
sections.content:
Rather than dictate a solution, the IAB and IESG conducted a thorough study. A consultant was hired to analyze the problem and propose several scenarios for how to restructure. The consultant's report identified four possible approaches:

Scenario A ("Leave it to ISOC"): Keep all administrative functions under ISOC's direct control. The community disliked this because it did not give the IETF enough say in its own operations.

Scenario B ("Increase IETF control through ISOC"): Try to get IETF representation on ISOC's board and committees to influence decisions. The community felt this was impractical—giving the IETF seats on an organization with many other priorities.

Scenario C ("Independent foundation"): Create a separate, independent nonprofit foundation (the IASF) to handle IETF administration. ISOC would continue to raise funds and handle standards process functions, but the new foundation would manage the day-to-day work. Some saw this as cleaner separation; others worried about financial risk and the complexity of creating a new legal entity.

Scenario D ("Complete independence"): Create a completely independent organization, separate from ISOC entirely. Few participants wanted this because it seemed too risky and would break a 20-year relationship with ISOC.

The IAB and IESG focused on Scenarios C and O (O was a new scenario developed during the process) as the most promising. In 2004, they presented both scenarios to the IETF community via email and invited a community poll. Roughly 40 participants contributed substantive comments; the poll showed stronger support for Scenario O, though not unanimity.
sections.plainLanguage: The leaders looked at four big ideas for how to fix things. Two seemed most reasonable: one that created a new independent company, and one that kept things mostly with ISOC but gave the IETF more control.

sections.title: Scenario C: An Independent Foundation
sections.content:
Scenario C proposed creating a new legal entity called the IETF Administrative Support Foundation (IASF), a nonprofit corporation incorporated in the U.S. state of Virginia. This independent corporation would manage all administrative support work for the IETF: meetings, contracts, finances, and relationships with the RFC Editor and IANA.

The IASF would be governed by a Board of Trustees (BoT) with seven members: one selected by the IAB, one by the IESG, two by ISOC, and three by the IETF community via the Nominating Committee. The board would hire an IETF Administrative Director (IAD) to run day-to-day operations.

ISOC would continue to raise funds for the IETF and play a role in the IETF standards process. However, ISOC would enter a formal contract with the IASF to fund it each year (around USD 900,000 ongoing, plus USD 600,000 for startup). The IASF would be separate, allowing the IETF to control its administrative operations without ISOC interference.

Advantages: Clear separation of concerns, IETF control, formal accountability structure.

Concerns: Creating a new legal entity requires lawyers, takes time, carries risks. ISOC board members worried it would complicate fundraising. Getting tax-exempt status would take months. The community expressed some worry about financial instability and what happens if the two organizations disagree.
sections.plainLanguage: Scenario C was like saying 'let's start a new company just for the IETF's office work.' It would have total control but also all the risks of running a company.

sections.title: Scenario O: IETF Control Within ISOC
sections.content:
Scenario O (called that because it was "neither A nor B", like blood type O) took a different approach. Instead of creating a new corporation, it proposed that the IETF's administrative support function stay within ISOC's legal structure but become an IETF-directed activity with oversight and control by the IETF community.

Under Scenario O, ISOC would house the IETF Administrative Support Activity (IASA), with a single full-time employee: the IETF Administrative Director (IAD). The IAD would be selected by and accountable to an IETF Administrative Oversight Committee (IAOC), also known as the IETF Administrative Oversight Committee.

The IAOC would have seven voting members: two chosen by the IETF Nominating Committee, one by the IESG, one by the IAB, one ex officio (the IETF Chair), and two appointed by ISOC. The IETF Chair leads the group, ensuring IETF community control. The IAB Chair would be a non-voting liaison.

Funding would come from three sources: IETF meeting fees, designated donations through ISOC, and a quarterly subsidy from ISOC's general funds. The goal was to eventually run on meeting fees and donations, with ISOC as a backstop.

Advantages: Lower risk (no new corporation to create), faster to implement, favorable tax status, keeps ISOC relationship intact, clearly defines the IETF's authority, can potentially be moved elsewhere later if needed.

Approach: The IAD handles day-to-day work and contracts. The IAOC provides oversight and approval. ISOC provides office space, legal standing, and financial backup. Each organization's role is clearly bounded.
sections.plainLanguage: Scenario O was like saying 'let's stay under ISOC's umbrella for the legal stuff, but put an IETF committee in charge of the office work.' Lower risk, easier to set up, but still gives the IETF control.

sections.title: Why Scenario O Was Chosen
sections.content:
The RFC outlines the reasoning for recommending Scenario O:

Consensus and Risk: The community poll showed stronger support for Scenario O than Scenario C. While not universal, more participants said they could live with O or strongly preferred it. For Scenario C, many participants said they were firmly convinced it was the wrong choice. In the IETF's consensus-based model, apparent drift of community opinion is a legitimate basis for a recommendation.

Speed and Tax Status: Creating a new corporation and obtaining 501(c)(3) nonprofit tax status could take months. Scenario O avoided this delay. A foundation doing administrative work (Scenario C) might face tax complications; a department within an existing nonprofit (Scenario O) would not.

Fundraising Risk: ISOC's Board worried that Scenario C's independent corporation might complicate their fundraising, since donors might see a disconnected entity. Scenario O kept ISOC as the fundraising organization, maintaining that relationship.

Workability: Although either scenario might work in principle, the RFC notes that Scenario O could be made to work faster and with less pain. The complexity of creating legal documents, securing lawyers, managing a new board structure, and transferring funds and contracts made Scenario C riskier and more time-consuming.

The IETF Chair announced the recommendation on October 8, 2004. The community approved it, and the IETF declared consensus on November 11, 2004.
sections.plainLanguage: When the leaders counted the votes and arguments, more people liked Scenario O. It was also faster to set up and had fewer legal risks. So they went with it.

sections.title: Implementation and Legacy
sections.content:
RFC 4089 publishes the recommendation for the record. The follow-up work was done in RFC 4071 and related documents, which formalized the structure and operational details of the IASA.

Scenario O was implemented successfully. The IASA was established within ISOC with an IAOC providing community oversight. The first IETF Administrative Director was hired, and the structure has managed IETF operations ever since.

The decision proved sound: it gave the IETF direct control over administrative functions, maintained the ISOC relationship, avoided the risks of creating a new legal entity, and established a model that is still in use. Later, when the IETF Community Governance and Conduct discussed potential separations or changes in the IETF/ISOC relationship, the clear boundaries established in Scenario O made those discussions possible without chaos.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF community said yes to Scenario O in late 2004, and it was put into practice. It worked well and is still how the IETF runs its business today.
